Guardians of the Coast: A Short History of Lighthouses For as long as people have sailed at night, they have needed some way of knowing where the land begins. The earliest aids to navigation were simply fires lit on hilltops or headlands, tended by local people who might be paid by passing merchants or, just as often, by nobody at all. The most famous early lighthouse, the Pharos of Alexandria, was completed in the third century BCE on a small island at the entrance to the city's harbour. Ancient writers described a tower of extraordinary height, and although estimates vary, many historians believe it stood around 100 metres tall. It survived for more than a thousand years before a series of earthquakes reduced it to ruins. For many centuries after the Pharos, lighthouses remained relatively rare. In medieval Europe, lights were often maintained by religious communities, who regarded the protection of sailors as a charitable duty. It was only with the great expansion of sea trade from the sixteenth century onwards that governments and merchants began to treat lighthouses as essential infrastructure. In England, a corporation known as Trinity House was granted a royal charter in 1514 and gradually took responsibility for lighthouses, buoys and pilots along much of the coast, a role it still performs today. Building lighthouses on exposed rocks presented enormous engineering challenges. The Eddystone reef, some 20 kilometres off the coast of Plymouth, illustrates this vividly. The first lighthouse there, an elaborate wooden structure designed by Henry Winstanley, was lit in 1698. Winstanley was so confident in his design that he expressed a wish to be inside it during the greatest storm ever known. In November 1703, he got his wish: he was visiting the lighthouse to carry out repairs when an exceptionally violent storm swept the tower away, killing Winstanley and everyone else inside. A second tower, also largely made of wood, burned down in 1755. The engineer John Smeaton, who designed the third Eddystone lighthouse, took a different approach. Inspired, according to his own account, by the shape of an oak tree, he built a tower that was broad at the base and narrowed towards the top, lowering its centre of gravity. Its granite blocks were cut so that they interlocked with one another, like pieces of a jigsaw, and they were bonded with a type of lime mortar that could set under water. Smeaton's tower, completed in 1759, stood for well over a century and became a model for lighthouse builders around the world. When erosion of the rock beneath it made a replacement necessary in the 1870s, the upper part of the tower was dismantled and rebuilt on land in Plymouth, where visitors can still climb it. Meanwhile, the light itself was improving. Early towers burned wood, coal or candles, and much of the light they produced escaped upwards or was absorbed by soot-blackened glass. In the late eighteenth century, oil lamps combined with curved metal reflectors made lights considerably brighter. The most significant breakthrough, however, came from the French physicist Augustin Fresnel. In the 1820s he developed a lens made of concentric rings of glass prisms, which captured a far greater proportion of the light from a lamp and bent it into a horizontal beam. A Fresnel lens could be seen from much further away than earlier lights while requiring much less fuel, and within a few decades such lenses had been installed in lighthouses across Europe and North America. Too Much of a Good Thing? Rethinking Choice Overload It has become something of a commonplace that modern consumers are overwhelmed by choice. Supermarkets stock tens of thousands of products, streaming services offer more films than anyone could watch in a lifetime, and even a cup of coffee can involve a bewildering series of decisions. Many commentators have argued that this abundance, far from making us happier, leaves us anxious and dissatisfied; some have even spoken of a 'tyranny of choice'. The idea has an intuitive appeal, but the scientific evidence behind it turns out to be more complicated than its popularity suggests. Much of the enthusiasm for the idea can be traced to a single experiment published in 2000 by the psychologists Sheena Iyengar and Mark Lepper. In an upmarket grocery store in California, they set up a tasting booth that displayed either 24 varieties of jam or just 6. The larger display attracted more shoppers: around 60 per cent of passers-by stopped at it, compared with 40 per cent for the smaller one. Yet when it came to buying, the pattern reversed. About 30 per cent of those who visited the small display went on to buy a jar, whereas only 3 per cent of those who visited the large display did so. (Visitors to either display received a discount coupon, which allowed the researchers to count purchases at the checkout.) The researchers concluded that too many options could discourage people from choosing at all, a phenomenon that came to be known as 'choice overload'. The study was elegant and its message memorable, and it quickly spread far beyond academic psychology. Business consultants advised companies to reduce their product ranges, and popular books argued that the explosion of consumer choice was contributing to unhappiness. In my view, the speed with which the finding was accepted owed as much to its appeal as a story as to the strength of the evidence. A single study, however striking, conducted in one shop over a short period, is a slender foundation on which to build general advice for entire industries. Subsequent research confirmed the need for caution. Some later experiments reproduced the effect, but others found no effect, and a few found the opposite: that people were more likely to make a choice, and more satisfied with their choices, when they had more options. In 2010, a team led by Benjamin Scheibehenne combined the results of 50 experiments in a statistical analysis known as a meta-analysis. They found that the average effect of choice overload across all of these studies was virtually zero. This did not mean that the original finding was wrong, but it did suggest that choice overload was far from a universal law of human behaviour. Some researchers also pointed out that studies with dramatic results are more likely to be published than studies that find nothing, a problem known as publication bias, which may have made the effect seem more consistent than it really was. Why might the effect appear in some situations and not others? Later work has begun to identify the conditions under which large assortments become a burden. A meta-analysis published in 2015 by Alexander Chernev and colleagues concluded that choice overload is more likely when the decision is difficult, when options are hard to compare, when people do not have clear preferences, and when they are trying to minimise the effort they spend deciding. A wine expert facing a long list of wines may relish the variety; a novice confronted with the same list may simply give up or pick at random. The way options are presented matters too: grouping products into categories, for instance, appears to make large assortments easier to navigate. What, then, should we conclude? It would be a mistake, I believe, to swing from one extreme to the other and declare that choice is never a problem. Most of us have experienced the paralysis of scrolling endlessly through options without settling on anything. But the evidence suggests that the problem lies less in the number of options than in the circumstances in which we confront them. Rather than simply reducing choice, businesses and policymakers might do better to help people choose: by organising options clearly, by offering sensible default options, or by providing tools that make comparison easier. There is also a broader lesson here about how psychological findings travel. The jam study was not a bad study; its authors were careful in describing what they had found. The problem was the eagerness of others to extract a simple rule from a single result. As psychology has become more aware of the need to replicate findings before treating them as established, the story of choice overload offers a useful reminder that the most memorable results are not always the most reliable. prompt.en: 11-14 minutes · 3 parts Speaking test The Speaking test is a face-to-face interview with an examiner and is recorded. It lasts 11-14 minutes. A recording of the examiner's prompts with timed pauses is provided in audio/speaking_examiner_prompts.mp3 for self-practice; record yourself answering. Part 1: Introduction and interview (4-5 minutes) The examiner asks about familiar topics. Topic: Your home town • Where is your home town? • What do you like most about it? • Has your home town changed much since you were a child? • Would you like to live there in the future? Why or why not? Topic: Weather • What kind of weather do you enjoy most? • Does the weather ever affect your mood? • What do people in your country usually do when it rains? • Would you prefer to live somewhere hotter or colder than where you live now? Part 2: Individual long turn (3-4 minutes, including 1 minute of preparation) Describe a time when you learned something new outside school or work. You should say: • what you learned • how and where you learned it • who, if anyone, helped you • and explain how you felt about learning it. You will have 1 minute to prepare and may make notes. Then speak for 1-2 minutes. The examiner may ask one brief follow-up question, e.g.: Do you still use this skill today? Part 3: Two-way discussion (4-5 minutes) Learning outside formal education • Why do you think many adults decide to learn new skills? • Is it better to learn a practical skill from a teacher or from online videos? • Do you think older people find it harder to learn new things? Why? Education and technology • How has technology changed the way people learn? • Some people say that schools should focus more on practical life skills. The Humble Pencil Few objects are as ordinary, or as quietly ingenious, as the pencil. It needs no ink, no batteries and no screen, and a single pencil can draw a line several kilometres long. Its story is usually said to begin in the sixteenth century in Borrowdale, a valley in the Lake District of northern England, where a deposit of unusually pure graphite was discovered. Local shepherds are said to have used lumps of the soft black mineral to mark their sheep, and before long it was being cut into sticks for writing and drawing. At the time, nobody understood what the substance was. Because it left a dark grey mark, it was widely believed to be a type of lead, and it was given names such as 'plumbago', from the Latin word for lead. Chemists showed in the late eighteenth century that graphite is in fact a form of carbon, but the old name stuck. We still speak of pencil 'lead' today, even though pencils have never contained the metal. Borrowdale graphite turned out to be valuable for more than writing. It was used to line the moulds in which cannonballs were cast, which gave the deposit military importance. Its owners guarded the mine closely; at times it was opened for only a few weeks each year to keep prices high, and in 1752 an Act of Parliament made the theft of graphite a serious crime. The earliest pencils were simply sticks of graphite wrapped in string or sheepskin to keep the user's fingers clean. Later, craftsmen began to insert the graphite into hollowed-out wooden holders. In Germany, where pure graphite was scarce, pencil makers in Nuremberg experimented with mixing powdered graphite with substances such as sulphur and glue, but the results were of poor quality, and English pencils remained the most highly prized in Europe. The decisive breakthrough came from France. In 1795, during the wars between France and Britain, French supplies of English graphite were cut off. The engineer Nicolas-Jacques Conté was asked to find an alternative, and he developed a method of mixing powdered graphite with clay, shaping the mixture into thin rods and firing them in a kiln. Conté's process had a further advantage: by changing the proportion of clay, manufacturers could control how hard or soft a pencil was. More clay produced a harder pencil that made a lighter line, while more graphite produced a softer, darker one. With only minor changes, this is the method still used today. Pencil making became a major industry in the nineteenth century. In the United States, manufacturers chose cedar for the wooden casing, because it was soft enough to sharpen easily and did not splinter. In 1858, a Philadelphia stationer named Hymen Lipman received a patent for a pencil with an eraser attached to one end. The patent was later declared invalid by the Supreme Court, which ruled that Lipman had merely combined two existing objects rather than inventing something new. By the end of the century, factories in Germany and the United States were turning out millions of pencils a year, using machines that cut grooves into thin slats of cedar, laid a graphite rod in each groove and glued a second slat on top before the whole sandwich was cut into individual pencils. Even the colour of the pencil has a story. According to a popular account, in the late nineteenth century some of the finest graphite came from a mine near the border between Siberia and China, and in China yellow was associated with royalty. One manufacturer painted its best pencils yellow to suggest this connection with quality, and the colour became so popular that in North America yellow is still the standard colour for pencils. Farming Upwards: The Promise and Problems of Vertical Farms A Imagine a farm with no fields, no tractors and no weather: a warehouse in the middle of a city, filled from floor to ceiling with shelves of lettuce growing under purple and white lights. This is a vertical farm. The idea of growing crops in stacked layers inside buildings was popularised around the turn of the twenty-first century by Dickson Despommier, a professor at Columbia University, who imagined skyscrapers that could feed entire neighbourhoods. Today most vertical farms are more modest, but the basic principles are the same: plants are grown indoors, usually without soil, with their roots in water containing dissolved nutrients, and with light supplied by energy-efficient LEDs. Growing plants under glass is of course nothing new, but traditional greenhouses rely on the sun, whereas a vertical farm replaces sunlight entirely and can therefore be built almost anywhere, from basements to old factories and shipping containers. B Supporters point to a long list of benefits. Because conditions are controlled, crops can be grown all year round, regardless of droughts, floods or frosts. Pests are largely kept out, so pesticides are rarely needed. Water use can be dramatically lower than in field agriculture, because the water is recycled within a closed system rather than draining away into the ground; some companies claim savings of more than 90 per cent. And because farms can be built close to the people who eat their produce, food can reach shops within hours of being harvested, reducing transport and waste. Some farms go further and spray the roots with a fine nutrient mist instead of immersing them, a technique known as aeroponics, which uses even less water. C The most serious drawback is energy. In a field, sunlight is free; in a vertical farm, every photon must be produced by electricity. Lighting, together with the heating, cooling and ventilation needed to keep conditions stable, makes vertical farms expensive to run. Their environmental impact therefore depends heavily on how their electricity is generated. A farm powered by coal may have a larger carbon footprint than a conventional farm hundreds of kilometres away, while one powered by renewable energy may compare well. Estimates vary from farm to farm, but electricity is commonly reported to be one of the largest single costs of running a vertical farm, often second only to labour. D Energy costs also limit what can be grown. Leafy greens such as lettuce, basil and other herbs are the mainstay of the industry, because they grow quickly, take up little space and command a high market value relative to their weight. Strawberries and tomatoes are grown by some companies. Staple crops are another matter. Wheat, rice and maize need a great deal of light to produce grain that sells for a low price per kilogram, and growing them indoors is, for now, far from economic. E These challenges became painfully clear in the early 2020s. Encouraged by investors, many vertical-farming companies expanded rapidly, building ever larger facilities. When energy prices rose sharply in 2022, several well-funded firms in Europe and North America closed farms, cut staff or went out of business altogether. Critics argued that the industry had promised too much, too soon, and that its business models had depended on cheap electricity and continued investment. Rising interest rates in the same period made it harder for young companies to raise new money, and some farms that had been built at great expense were sold for a fraction of their cost. READING PASSAGE 3 (Questions 27-40) You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27-40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below. In Defence of Boredom Boredom has a bad reputation. We tend to treat it as an unpleasant state to be escaped as quickly as possible, and modern life offers endless means of escape: at the first hint of tedium in a queue or on a train, most of us reach for our phones. Yet in recent years a number of psychologists and philosophers have argued that boredom is not simply a nuisance but an emotion with a purpose. I am not convinced that boredom is the hidden blessing some popular writers now claim, but I do think it deserves a fairer hearing than it usually receives. Part of the difficulty is that boredom is surprisingly hard to define. People use the word to describe everything from mild restlessness to deep despair. In 2012, the psychologist John Eastwood and his colleagues proposed that boredom is best understood as the unpleasant experience of wanting to engage in satisfying activity but being unable to do so. This seems to me a genuinely useful definition, because it explains why boredom feels uncomfortable rather than merely neutral: it involves a frustrated desire, not just an absence of stimulation. Just how uncomfortable boredom can be was shown in a much-discussed series of studies published in 2014 by Timothy Wilson and his team at the University of Virginia. Participants were asked to sit alone in a bare room for between six and fifteen minutes, with nothing to do but think. Most found the experience unpleasant. In one version of the study, participants were given the option of pressing a button to give themselves a mild electric shock, which they had earlier said they would pay money to avoid. Twelve of the eighteen men and six of the twenty-four women chose to shock themselves at least once rather than simply sit with their thoughts. Why would evolution have equipped us with such an unpleasant feeling? One answer, developed by the philosopher Andreas Elpidorou among others, is that boredom works rather like pain or hunger. Pain tells us that something is damaging our body; hunger tells us that we need food. Boredom, on this view, tells us that our current situation is failing to engage us and that we should look for something different. Seen this way, boredom is not an enemy but a signal, and it can push people towards goals that are more meaningful to them. Some researchers have gone further and suggested that boredom can make people more creative. In one well-known experiment, the psychologists Sandi Mann and Rebekah Cadman asked one group of participants to spend fifteen minutes copying telephone numbers from a directory, a deliberately dull task, while a control group did nothing beforehand. Both groups were then asked to think of as many uses as possible for a pair of plastic cups. The participants who had been bored first came up with more ideas. The result is intriguing, but it should be treated with caution: the studies involved small numbers of people, and later attempts to find similar effects have produced mixed results. It would also be a mistake to romanticise boredom. Researchers distinguish between boredom as a passing state, which everyone experiences, and boredom proneness, a lasting tendency to feel bored frequently. People who are highly prone to boredom are more likely to report problems such as overeating, gambling and poor performance at school or work. In jobs that require constant attention but offer little variety, such as monitoring screens, boredom can also lead to dangerous mistakes. What, then, of smartphones? It would be too simple to blame technology for every difficulty we have in tolerating boredom; people complained of tedium long before the invention of the telephone. But constant access to entertainment may prevent boredom from doing its job. If we silence the signal the moment it appears, we never discover where it might have led us. For this reason, I believe that children in particular benefit from some unstructured time in which they are left to find their own amusement, even if they complain about it at first. Boredom, in the end, is neither good nor bad in itself. Like other uncomfortable emotions, it carries information, and its value depends on how we respond to it. The Great Stink and the Making of Modern London In the summer of 1858, London smelled so bad that Parliament could barely function. For decades, the city's sewage had flowed, largely untreated, into the River Thames, and an unusually hot, dry June turned the river into an open sewer. Newspapers called it 'the Great Stink'. In the newly rebuilt Houses of Parliament, which stand on the riverbank, the curtains were soaked in chloride of lime in an attempt to mask the smell, and some members talked of moving Parliament out of London altogether. The problem had been growing for years. London's population had more than doubled in the first half of the nineteenth century, to around 2.5 million people. Ironically, an innovation intended to improve hygiene had made matters worse: the flushing toilet, which became increasingly popular from the 1840s, sent far larger volumes of water and waste into the old drains and cesspits, which overflowed into streets and streams and, ultimately, into the Thames, from which many Londoners still drew their drinking water. Some of the smaller rivers that had once flowed openly through the city, such as the Fleet, had in effect become sewers themselves. The city had already suffered repeated outbreaks of cholera. An epidemic in 1849 killed around 14,000 Londoners, and another in 1853 and 1854 killed more than 10,000. At the time, most doctors and officials believed that diseases such as cholera were spread by 'miasma', or bad air, rather than by contaminated water. Paradoxically, this mistaken belief helped to bring about reform: if foul smells caused disease, then the stench rising from the Thames was not merely unpleasant but deadly, and something had to be done. Once politicians themselves were suffering, action came quickly. Within a matter of weeks, Parliament passed legislation giving the Metropolitan Board of Works the power and the funds to build a new sewer system. The task fell to the Board's chief engineer, Joseph Bazalgette, who had already drawn up plans for such a system but had struggled to win approval for them. The legislation allowed the Board to borrow some £3 million, an enormous sum at the time, and construction began the following year. Bazalgette's solution was to intercept the sewage before it reached the Thames. He designed a network of large brick sewers running parallel to the river, which collected waste from the older sewers and carried it eastwards, mostly by gravity, to outfalls far downstream of the centre of London. Where gravity alone was insufficient, huge pumping stations, such as those at Abbey Mills and Crossness, lifted the sewage to a higher level. In all, the project involved around 130 kilometres of main intercepting sewers and some 1,800 kilometres of smaller street sewers. Thousands of labourers were employed, and although the main system was opened in stages during the 1860s, the work was not fully completed until the mid-1870s. Bazalgette is remembered for his foresight. When calculating the size of the pipes, he estimated the volume of sewage the population would produce and then, according to a well-known story, doubled the diameter, reasoning that the work would only be done once. That decision allowed the system to cope with a population far larger than he could have imagined. He also insisted on the use of Portland cement, which was stronger than conventional mortar and became harder when exposed to water, although it was more expensive. The Language of the Hive A A honeybee that has found a rich patch of flowers faces a problem. The food is out in the landscape, perhaps several kilometres away, but the bees that could help collect it are in the dark interior of the hive. In the 1940s, the Austrian zoologist Karl von Frisch announced a remarkable solution. Beekeepers had long noticed bees moving excitedly on the comb, but no one had understood the meaning of these movements. According to von Frisch, the returning forager performs a dance on the vertical surface of the honeycomb that tells her nestmates where the food is. Von Frisch spent decades refining his interpretation, and in 1973 he shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with two other pioneers of the study of animal behaviour. B The most informative movement is the 'waggle run'. The dancing bee moves forward in a straight line while vigorously shaking her abdomen from side to side, then circles back to her starting point and repeats the run, alternating between a right-hand and a left-hand return loop. The angle of the waggle run relative to the vertical indicates the direction of the food relative to the sun: a run straight upwards means 'fly towards the sun', while a run pointing 40 degrees to the right of vertical means 'fly 40 degrees to the right of the sun'. The duration of the waggle run indicates distance; the longer it lasts, the further away the food. A single dance may contain dozens of waggle runs, and a particularly rich food source can keep a forager dancing for several minutes. C Remarkably, bees take account of the sun's movement across the sky. A forager that has been inside the hive for some time will adjust the angle of her dance to allow for how far the sun has moved since she was last outside. Bees can also determine the sun's position on cloudy days, as long as some patches of blue sky are visible, because they can detect patterns of polarised light that are invisible to humans. Experiments in which hives were moved to unfamiliar locations, or in which bees were shown artificial patterns of polarised light, have confirmed how flexible this navigational system is. D Not everyone accepted von Frisch's ideas. In the 1960s, the American biologist Adrian Wenner argued that recruited bees found food mainly by following its scent, and by the odour carried on the dancer's body, rather than by decoding the dance. The debate continued for years. It was largely settled by two kinds of experiment. In the early 1990s, researchers built a robotic bee that could perform dances inside a hive, and showed that recruits flew in the direction it indicated. Then, in 2005, scientists attached tiny radar transponders to recruited bees and tracked their flights, finding that they flew directly towards the location signalled by the dance, although they often relied on scent to pinpoint the food once they were nearby. Another puzzle, how recruits can perceive a dance in the darkness of the hive, has also been answered: they follow the dancer closely, detecting her movements and the vibrations she produces with their antennae. E The dance is not entirely innate. In a study published in 2023, researchers raised colonies in which young bees were unable to observe experienced dancers before they began dancing themselves. These bees produced dances that were noticeably less accurate, especially in signalling distance. Although their performance improved with practice, some errors persisted, suggesting that social learning plays a part in bee communication, as it does in the songs of many birds. Can We Trust What Witnesses Remember? For much of legal history, an eyewitness who confidently identified a suspect was regarded as among the most persuasive forms of evidence. Juries find such testimony compelling, and it is easy to see why: a person who saw a crime with their own eyes seems far more reliable than a chain of circumstantial clues. Yet over the past fifty years, psychological research has shown that human memory is far less like a video recording than most people assume. In my view, this research has rightly changed how courts treat eyewitness evidence, although some of the popular conclusions drawn from it go too far. Much of the early work was carried out by the American psychologist Elizabeth Loftus. In a classic study published in 1974, Loftus and John Palmer showed participants films of traffic accidents and then asked them how fast the cars had been going. The wording of the question mattered: participants asked how fast the cars were going when they 'smashed' into each other gave higher estimates of speed than those asked about cars that 'hit' each other. A week later, participants who had heard the word 'smashed' were also more likely to report having seen broken glass, even though there had been none in the film. Later studies went further, showing that it is possible to create memories of entire events that never happened. In one well-known experiment, a minority of adult participants, given false accounts said to come from their relatives, came to believe that as children they had been lost in a shopping centre. Findings like these led many people to conclude that memory is hopelessly unreliable. I think that conclusion is mistaken. What the research shows is that memory is reconstructive: each time we recall an event, we rebuild it from fragments, and the rebuilding can be influenced by what we have learned since. This makes memory vulnerable, but it does not make it worthless. The real-world consequences of memory errors have nonetheless been serious. Since the 1990s, DNA testing has led to the release of hundreds of people in the United States who had been wrongly convicted of serious crimes. According to the Innocence Project, an organisation that works on such cases, mistaken eyewitness identification played a part in roughly seven out of ten of these convictions. In most of these cases, the witnesses were not lying: they sincerely believed they were identifying the right person. One reason for these errors lies in the way identifications were traditionally obtained. In a typical line-up, a witness views a suspect alongside several other people and is asked whether the culprit is present. If the police officer running the line-up knows which person is the suspect, he or she may unintentionally signal this through words or body language. Witnesses who are told afterwards that they have chosen correctly tend to become more confident, and by the time a case reaches court, a hesitant initial choice may have become a certainty. This last point has led to a significant change in thinking about confidence. For many years, researchers argued that a witness's confidence was a poor guide to accuracy. More recent analyses, notably by the psychologists John Wixted and Gary Wells, suggest that the picture is more nuanced. Confidence expressed at the time of a witness's first identification, under fair conditions, can be a reasonably good indicator of accuracy; it is confidence that has grown later, through feedback and repetition, that is misleading. I find this argument convincing, and it has clear practical implications. Many police forces have now adopted reforms based on this research. Line-ups are increasingly run on a 'double-blind' basis, by an officer who does not know which person is the suspect. Witnesses are warned that the culprit may not be present, and their level of confidence is recorded immediately, in their own words, before they receive any feedback. These procedures do not eliminate error, but they make it much less likely that a witness's memory will be shaped by the investigation itself. Eyewitness testimony, then, should be neither blindly trusted nor automatically dismissed. Memory is a remarkable but imperfect system, and the task for the legal system is to collect and evaluate it in ways that respect both its strengths and its weaknesses. prompt.en: 60 minutes · 3 passages · 40 questions Read the three passages and answer Questions 1-40. You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Transfer time is NOT added at the end of the Reading test. READING PASSAGE 1 (Questions 1-13) You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1-13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below. The Race to the South Pole In the early twentieth century, the South Pole was one of the last great prizes of exploration. Its location was known precisely, at the centre of a vast, ice-covered continent, but no one had ever reached it. In 1910, two expeditions set out with that goal: a British team led by the naval officer Robert Falcon Scott, and a Norwegian team led by Roald Amundsen, who was already celebrated for having navigated the Northwest Passage. Amundsen had not originally intended to go south at all. His plan had been to drift across the Arctic Ocean towards the North Pole in his ship, the Fram. But in 1909 two Americans, Frederick Cook and Robert Peary, each claimed to have reached the North Pole, and Amundsen secretly changed his destination. Only when the Fram reached Madeira did he reveal the new plan to his crew, and he sent Scott a brief telegram informing him that the Fram was 'proceeding Antarctic'. The two expeditions established their bases on opposite sides of the Ross Ice Shelf. Scott returned to McMurdo Sound, where earlier British expeditions had worked, and built a hut at Cape Evans. Amundsen chose the Bay of Whales, an inlet in the ice shelf itself that was about 100 kilometres closer to the Pole. Some experts had warned that the ice there might break away into the sea, but Amundsen judged that it rested on solid ground and would remain stable, and he was right. During the months before the polar journey, his men also laid depots of food along the first part of the route, marking each one with a long line of flags so that it could be found even in poor visibility. The most important difference between the expeditions lay in their methods of transport. Amundsen relied almost entirely on dogs. He and his men were expert skiers, and they had learned techniques of polar travel from the Inuit during earlier journeys in the Arctic. As the journey progressed, some of the dogs were killed to feed the others and the men, a grim but carefully planned part of the strategy. Scott, by contrast, took a mixture of motor sledges, ponies and dogs, intending that his men would haul the sledges themselves for much of the way. The motor sledges broke down early, and the ponies, poorly suited to the conditions, all died or had to be shot before reaching the high plateau. Amundsen's team of five men reached the South Pole on 14 December 1911. They spent three days there, taking measurements to make sure that they had truly reached the Pole, and left a small tent containing a letter for Scott, asking him to forward a message to the King of Norway in case they failed to return. They then travelled back to their base without serious difficulty, arriving in late January 1912. The Norwegians named their camp at the Pole Polheim, and Amundsen later wrote that the journey had gone almost exactly according to plan. Scott's party of five reached the Pole on 17 January 1912, more than a month later, only to find the Norwegian tent and flag. 'Great God! This is an awful place,' Scott wrote in his diary. The return journey became a disaster. The men were exhausted, short of food and fuel, and suffering from frostbite. Edgar Evans died in February. In March, Lawrence Oates, whose feet were badly frostbitten, walked out of the tent into a blizzard, apparently so as not to slow down his companions. Scott, Edward Wilson and Henry Bowers died in their tent around the end of March, about 18 kilometres from a large store of supplies. Their bodies were found by a search party the following November. For decades afterwards, Scott was celebrated in Britain as a tragic hero, while Amundsen's achievement received less

Working Less, Achieving More? The Four-Day Week The idea that people might one day work far fewer hours is not new. In 1930, the economist John Maynard Keynes predicted that within a century, rising productivity would allow his grandchildren's generation to work around fifteen hours a week. That prediction has not come true; in most wealthy countries, the standard working week has barely changed for decades. In recent years, however, a growing movement has argued for a four-day week without any loss of pay, and a series of trials has given the idea a credibility it previously lacked. I believe the evidence so far is genuinely encouraging, though it is not yet as conclusive as some campaigners suggest. The best-known trial took place in the United Kingdom in the second half of 2022. Sixty-one companies, employing around 2,900 people, agreed to reduce working time by about a fifth for six months, while paying staff the same. The organisations involved ranged from software firms and marketing agencies to a fish-and-chip shop. At the end of the trial, 56 of the 61 companies chose to continue with a shorter week, and 18 said that the change was permanent. Revenue, on average, stayed broadly the same, while employees reported less stress and burnout, better sleep and an easier balance between work and family life. Earlier, between 2015 and 2019, two large trials in Iceland had reduced the working week of more than 2,500 public-sector workers, from 40 hours to 35 or 36, again without any cut in pay. Researchers who analysed the results reported that productivity and service provision remained the same or improved in most workplaces, and the trials were followed by agreements that gave many Icelandic workers the right to shorter hours. These results are often cited, quite reasonably, as evidence that reduced hours can work in the public sector as well as in private business. How can people produce as much in four days as in five? Supporters offer several explanations. Long hours do not necessarily mean more output: tired workers make more mistakes, and much time in a typical office is lost to unnecessary meetings and distractions. When the working week is shortened, organisations are forced to look closely at how time is used. Many companies in the trials cut the length and number of meetings, introduced periods of uninterrupted work, and automated routine tasks. In this sense, the four-day week is less a gift of leisure than a demand for greater efficiency. There are, however, good reasons for caution. The companies that took part in the trials volunteered to do so, and they are likely to have been those most enthusiastic about the idea and most able to make it work. Their experience may not be typical of businesses in general. Moreover, six months is a short period; it is possible that the initial enthusiasm of managers and staff will fade, or that the pressure to fit five days' work into four will itself become a source of stress. Some employees in the trials did indeed report that their days had become more intense. The model also suits some jobs better than others. In office work, where tasks can often be reorganised, a shorter week may be achieved through greater efficiency. But in hospitals, schools, shops and factories, output depends heavily on the number of hours that staff are present. Reducing hours in these sectors without reducing pay would usually require hiring more people, which would increase costs. Some organisations have responded by offering a 'compressed' week, in which staff work the same number of hours over four longer days. In my view, this is not really a four-day week at all, and it may suit few employees with caring responsibilities. None of these difficulties is a reason to dismiss the idea. The trials so far suggest that, for many organisations, a shorter week can benefit employees without harming the business. What is needed now is longer and more varied research, including companies that have not volunteered, so that we can see which kinds of work benefit and which do not. Keynes's fifteen-hour week may remain a distant dream, but a four-day week for many workers no longer seems an unrealistic one. Whether it spreads will depend less on slogans than on careful evidence. Questions 27-30: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

Many companies in the trials cut the length and number of meetings, introduced periods of uninterrupted work, and automated routine tasks. In this sense, the four-day week is less a gift of leisure than a demand for greater efficiency. There are, however, good reasons for caution. The companies that took part in the trials volunteered to do so, and they are likely to have been those most enthusiastic about the idea and most able to make it work. Their experience may not be typical of businesses in general. Moreover, six months is a short period; it is possible that the initial enthusiasm of managers and staff will fade, or that the pressure to fit five days' work into four will itself become a source of stress. Some employees in the trials did indeed report that their days had become more intense. The model also suits some jobs better than others. In office work, where tasks can often be reorganised, a shorter week may be achieved through greater efficiency. But in hospitals, schools, shops and factories, output depends heavily on the number of hours that staff are present. Reducing hours in these sectors without reducing pay would usually require hiring more people, which would increase costs. Some organisations have responded by offering a 'compressed' week, in which staff work the same number of hours over

A Penny for Your Letter: The Birth of the Postage Stamp Today it seems obvious that the person who sends a letter should pay for it, and that the price should be the same whether the letter travels across the street or across the country. In Britain before 1840, however, neither of these principles applied. Postage was normally paid by the person who received a letter, not by the sender, and the charge depended on the distance the letter had travelled and on the number of sheets of paper it contained. Sending a single sheet from London to Edinburgh could cost more than a shilling, a significant part of a labourer's daily wage, and many ordinary people simply could not afford to write to distant relatives. The system also encouraged a good deal of cheating. Because the recipient paid, people developed ways of communicating without paying at all. A sender might write small symbols or a pattern of dots on the outside of the folded letter; the recipient would look at the outside, understand the message, and then refuse to accept the letter, leaving the Post Office to carry it for nothing. Members of Parliament, meanwhile, enjoyed the right to send letters free of charge, and this privilege was widely abused, with MPs signing letters on behalf of friends and businesses. The man who proposed a solution was not a postal official. Rowland Hill was a former schoolmaster with a keen interest in social reform and a talent for working with numbers. In 1837 he published a pamphlet entitled Post Office Reform: Its Importance and Practicability. Hill had studied the Post Office's own figures and concluded that the actual cost of carrying a letter was tiny compared with the cost of handling it, recording the charge and collecting payment. Distance, he argued, made very little difference. He proposed that all letters weighing up to half an ounce should be carried anywhere in the country for a single, low charge of one penny, and that this should be paid in advance by the sender. To show that payment had been made, Hill suggested using 'a bit of paper just large enough to bear the stamp, and covered at the back with a glutinous wash'. Senior figures in the Post Office were strongly opposed to the scheme, warning that the cheap rate would ruin its finances. But Hill's ideas were enthusiastically supported by merchants and campaigners, and public pressure eventually persuaded Parliament to act. The Uniform Penny Post was introduced on 10 January 1840, and the free-postage privilege of MPs was abolished at the same time. The world's first adhesive postage stamp, later known as the Penny Black, became valid for use on 6 May 1840. It showed the profile of the young Queen Victoria, based on a medal that had been made to mark her visit to the City of London, and it was printed in black ink. To make forgery more difficult, the design included a finely engraved background, and each stamp carried a different pair of letters in its lower corners, showing its position on the printed sheet. There were no perforations: post office clerks had to cut the stamps from the sheet with scissors, and machines for perforating sheets were not introduced until the 1850s. Alongside the stamp, the Post Office issued prepaid envelopes and letter sheets illustrated by the artist William Mulready. His design showed a figure representing Britannia sending messengers to every part of the world. The public found it pompous, and it was so widely mocked in cartoons that it was soon withdrawn. Lost Without It? Satellite Navigation and the Human Sense of Direction Not long ago, finding your way around an unfamiliar city meant unfolding a paper map, working out where you were and planning a route. Today most people simply type a destination into a phone and follow the blue dot. Satellite navigation has made getting lost far less common, and it has undoubtedly saved travellers a great deal of time and stress. Yet a growing body of research suggests that this convenience may come at a price. When we hand the job of navigation to a machine, we may be giving up a skill that we are in danger of losing. To understand why, it helps to know how people normally find their way. Psychologists distinguish between two broad strategies. In the first, a person learns a sequence of actions: turn left at the bakery, go straight on past the church, take the second right. In the second, the person builds a mental map of the area, an understanding of where places are in relation to one another, which allows them to work out new routes and shortcuts. The second strategy is more flexible, and it depends heavily on a part of the brain called the hippocampus. Several studies have examined what happens to this system when people rely on navigation devices. In one experiment in Japan, researchers asked three groups of participants to walk to a series of destinations: one group used satellite navigation, another used a paper map, and a third had been shown the route in person beforehand. Those using satellite navigation walked further, stopped more often, and afterwards drew less accurate sketches of the area than either of the other groups. In another study, carried out in London, people's brain activity was recorded while they navigated a virtual version of a district of the city. Activity in the hippocampus increased when participants had to choose a route for themselves, but it largely disappeared when they were simply following instructions. These findings fit with what we know about the brain more generally. Like a muscle, the brain tends to strengthen the abilities that are used and to neglect those that are not. A study in Canada that followed a group of adults for three years found that those who used satellite navigation most heavily showed a steeper decline in spatial memory over that period. Importantly, the researchers found no evidence that people with a poor sense of direction were simply more likely to use the devices. This suggests, although it does not prove, that heavy use of navigation technology was itself responsible for some of the decline. It would be wrong to conclude from this that satellite navigation is harmful in itself or that we should abandon it. The technology has clear benefits, particularly for drivers, who are safer when they can concentrate on the road rather than on a map, and for people with conditions that make navigation genuinely difficult. In emergencies, it can be life-saving. In my view, the problem is not the technology but the way most of us use it: passively, without paying any attention to where we are going. There are simple ways to use satellite navigation more actively. Before setting off, travellers can look at the whole route on the map and note a few landmarks. During the journey, they can try to predict the next turn before the device announces it. Some researchers have proposed that devices themselves could be redesigned to encourage this, for example by showing nearby landmarks prominently or by giving directions in terms of the surroundings rather than distances. Children, in particular, should be given regular opportunities to find their way without a device, since the skills of navigation develop through practice in childhood. Some commentators argue that worrying about navigation skills is pointless, because machines will always be there to guide us. This seems to me too optimistic. Batteries die, signals fail in tunnels and remote areas, and devices sometimes give instructions that are plainly wrong. More importantly, the ability to form a mental map of the world is linked to the brain systems we use for memory more generally. Keeping those systems active may matter for reasons that go well beyond finding our way to the station. Questions 27-30: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

prompt.en: 11-14 minutes · 3 parts Speaking test The Speaking test is a face-to-face interview with an examiner and is recorded. It lasts 11-14 minutes. A recording of the examiner's prompts with timed pauses is provided in audio/speaking_examiner_prompts.mp3 for self-practice; record yourself answering. Part 1: Introduction and interview (4-5 minutes) The examiner asks about familiar topics. Topic: Neighbours • Do you know your neighbours well? • How often do you talk to your neighbours? • Have you ever helped a neighbour? • What makes someone a good neighbour? Topic: Weekends • What do you usually do at the weekend? • Do you prefer busy or relaxing weekends? • How were your weekends different when you were a child? • Is there anything you would like to do at weekends but don't have time for? Part 2: Individual long turn (3-4 minutes, including 1 minute of preparation) Describe a journey you remember well. You should say: • where you went • who you travelled with • how you travelled • and explain why you remember this journey so well. You will have 1 minute to prepare and may make notes. Then speak for 1-2 minutes. The examiner may ask one brief follow-up question, e.g.: Would you like to make the same journey again? Part 3: Two-way discussion (4-5 minutes) Travel • Why do some people prefer to travel on their own? • How has the way people go on holiday changed in recent years? • Do you think people learn more from travelling than from books? Journeys in the future • How might long-distance travel change in the next few decades? • Should governments discourage people from flying? • Will people still need to travel for work in the future, or will technology replace it? END OF TEST

Sealed for Later: The Invention of Canned Food For most of human history, keeping food from spoiling was a constant struggle. People dried, salted, smoked and pickled meat, fish and vegetables, but all of these methods changed the taste and texture of the food, and none of them worked for everything. The problem was especially serious for armies and navies, which had to feed large numbers of men far from home. Sailors on long voyages lived largely on salted meat and hard biscuits, and many suffered from diseases caused by poor diet. In 1795, the French government, then at war with much of Europe, offered a prize of 12,000 francs to anyone who could find a better way of preserving food for its soldiers and sailors. The man who eventually won the prize was not a scientist. Nicolas Appert was a Paris confectioner and chef who had spent years working with sugar, syrups and preserved fruit. Over more than a decade of experiments, he developed a simple but effective method. Food was placed in thick glass bottles, which were sealed tightly with cork and wax and then heated in boiling water for a period that depended on the type of food. As long as the seal remained unbroken, the contents stayed edible for months or even years. Appert set up a small factory outside Paris, and some years before the prize was awarded, samples of his preserved food were sent to sea with the French navy, where they were found to be in excellent condition after several months. In 1810, Appert was awarded the prize, on condition that he publish a full description of his method. The book that followed explained in detail how to preserve dozens of foods, from soups and meat to vegetables, fruit and milk. What Appert could not explain was why his method worked. Like most people of his time, he believed that food spoiled because of contact with air. It was not until the 1860s that the French scientist Louis Pasteur showed that decay is caused by microorganisms, and that heating kills them while the seal prevents new ones from entering. Appert's glass bottles had an obvious weakness: they broke easily, which made them impractical for armies on the move. The solution came from Britain. In the same year that Appert received his prize, a merchant named Peter Durand was granted a patent for preserving food in containers made of glass, pottery or tin-plated iron. Durand does not appear to have produced any canned food himself. Instead, he sold the patent, and in 1812 the engineer Bryan Donkin and his partner John Hall opened a factory in London that produced food in iron cans coated with tin. Within a few years, the factory was supplying the Royal Navy, and canned meat and soup were being carried on voyages of exploration to the Arctic. Early cans were very different from those we know today. Each one was made by hand by a skilled worker, who cut the metal, shaped it and sealed the joins with solder, producing only a handful of cans an hour. The cans were thick and heavy, sometimes weighing more than the food inside, and they were not easy to open. One set of instructions advised the user to cut round the top with a chisel and hammer. Soldiers sometimes used bayonets or knives, or even fired bullets at the cans. Surprisingly, the first tool designed specifically for opening cans did not appear until the 1850s, more than forty years after the first cans were made, by which time manufacturers had begun to use thinner metal. Canned food was not always safe. The solder used to seal early cans contained lead, which could pass into the food. The Puzzle of the Yawn A Few behaviours are as familiar, or as poorly understood, as the yawn. Almost all vertebrates yawn, including mammals, birds, reptiles and fish, which suggests that the behaviour is extremely old in evolutionary terms. Humans begin yawning before they are born: ultrasound scans have shown babies yawning in the womb from around the eleventh week of pregnancy. A typical yawn lasts about six seconds and follows a fixed sequence, a long, deep breath in with the jaw wide open, a brief pause at the peak, and a shorter breath out, and once it has started it is very difficult to stop. Yawning is not simply a sign of tiredness, either. People yawn most often shortly after waking and before going to sleep, but athletes, musicians and students often report yawning just before a race, a performance or an examination, when they are anxious and not at all sleepy. B The most common explanation offered for yawning is that it brings extra oxygen into the body, or removes excess carbon dioxide, when we are tired or bored. This idea was tested in the 1980s by the psychologist Robert Provine. He asked volunteers to breathe air containing different amounts of oxygen and carbon dioxide and recorded how often they yawned. Breathing air rich in carbon dioxide made people breathe faster, but it did not make them yawn more, and breathing pure oxygen did not make them yawn less. Provine concluded that yawning and breathing are controlled by separate mechanisms, and the oxygen theory has largely been abandoned by researchers, even though it remains popular with the general public. C A more recent theory, developed by the psychologist Andrew Gallup and his colleagues, proposes that yawning helps to cool the brain. The brain works best within a narrow range of temperatures, and the deep breath taken during a yawn, together with the stretching of the jaw, increases blood flow to the skull and brings in cooler air. In support of this idea, researchers have found that people yawned less often when they held a cold pack against their foreheads, or when they breathed through their noses, which cools the blood going to the brain, than when they held a warm pack or breathed through their mouths. D The cooling theory also makes a surprising prediction: people should yawn less when the air around them is either very hot or very cold. If the air is as warm as the body, breathing it in cannot cool the brain, and if it is freezing, cooling is unnecessary and may even be harmful. A study carried out in Arizona found that people yawned more often in winter, when the air was mild, than in summer, when temperatures were close to body temperature. A later study in Vienna found the reverse pattern, with more yawning in summer, which also fitted the prediction, because summers in Vienna are mild rather than hot. Not everyone accepts the theory, but these results are difficult to explain in other ways. E Perhaps the strangest feature of yawning is that it is contagious. Seeing someone else yawn, hearing a yawn, or even reading about yawning, as you may be noticing now, can trigger a yawn. Contagious yawning has been observed in chimpanzees and bonobos, and some studies have found that dogs yawn after watching their owners yawn. In humans, it develops relatively late. Young children rarely catch yawns from others, and the behaviour becomes common only from about the age of four or five. Even among adults, the tendency varies greatly: when volunteers watch videos of people yawning, some yawn again and again, while others do not yawn at all. This idea was tested in the 1980s by the psychologist Robert Provine. He asked volunteers to breathe air containing different amounts of oxygen and carbon dioxide and recorded how often they yawned. Breathing air rich in carbon dioxide made people breathe faster, but it did not make them yawn more, and breathing pure oxygen did not make them yawn less. Provine concluded that yawning and breathing are controlled by separate mechanisms, and the oxygen theory has largely been abandoned by researchers, even though it remains popular with the general public. The brain works best within a narrow range of temperatures, and the deep breath taken during a yawn, together with the stretching of the jaw, increases blood flow to the skull and brings in cooler air. Science for Everyone? The Rise of Citizen Science In 2007, a group of astronomers at the University of Oxford faced a problem. A telescope survey had produced images of around a million galaxies, and the researchers wanted to classify them according to their shape. Computers at the time could not do this reliably, and a single scientist working full-time would have needed years to look at them all. So the team launched a website called Galaxy Zoo, inviting members of the public to classify the galaxies themselves. Within a day of its launch, volunteers were classifying tens of thousands of galaxies an hour, and within a year more than a hundred thousand people had taken part. Each galaxy was classified many times by different people, and the combined results proved to be as accurate as those of professional astronomers. Galaxy Zoo is often described as the beginning of modern citizen science, but the idea of ordinary people contributing to research is much older. For more than a century, amateur birdwatchers in North America have taken part in an annual bird count, and their records now form one of the longest-running sources of information about changes in bird populations. Weather records kept by volunteers, observations of the first flowers of spring and amateur discoveries of comets have all made important contributions to science. What the internet has changed is the scale. Projects can now involve hundreds of thousands of people around the world, and smartphones allow volunteers to submit photographs, recordings and precise locations instantly. The benefits for scientists are obvious. Volunteers can collect data across areas far larger than any research team could cover, and they can process quantities of information that would otherwise be impossible to handle. In some cases, they have done more than simply provide labour. In 2011, players of an online puzzle game called Foldit, in which participants compete to fold protein molecules into their most stable shapes, worked out the structure of an enzyme from a virus related to HIV within three weeks, a problem that had defeated scientists for more than a decade. Volunteers have also made unexpected discoveries: one Galaxy Zoo participant, a Dutch schoolteacher, noticed an unusual glowing cloud of gas that turned out to be a previously unknown kind of astronomical object. There are also benefits for the volunteers and for society as a whole. People who take part in citizen science projects often say that they have learned a great deal, and some studies suggest that participation can increase people's understanding of how science works and their trust in scientific findings. In a period when scientific expertise is sometimes treated with suspicion, this seems to me one of the strongest arguments for encouraging such projects. Citizen science can also give local communities a voice: groups living near factories or busy roads have used their own measurements of air or water quality to persuade authorities to take action. Nevertheless, citizen science has its critics, and some of their concerns deserve to be taken seriously. The most common is that data collected by untrained volunteers may be unreliable. In practice, well-designed projects deal with this problem in several ways, for example by having each item checked by several people, by providing training and clear instructions, and by using statistical methods to identify unusual results. Studies comparing volunteer data with that of professionals have generally found that the quality is high, although it varies considerably between projects. A more difficult question concerns fairness. Volunteers give their time for free, and the results of their work are published in scientific journals, sometimes contributing to the careers of the professional scientists involved. Some projects now list volunteers as co-authors or thank them by name, but many do not. I believe that research institutions have a responsibility to recognise volunteers' contributions properly and to make the results of projects freely available to those who helped to produce them. If citizen science is seen simply as a source of free labour, it risks losing the goodwill on which it depends. Citizen science will not replace professional research, and nor should it. Many scientific questions require specialist knowledge, expensive equipment and years of training. Transfer time is NOT added at the end of the Reading test. READING PASSAGE 1 (Questions 1-13) You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1-13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below. The Ice King: How Frozen Ponds Became a Global Business In the early nineteenth century, ice was a luxury that most of the world had never seen. In cold regions, people had long cut blocks from frozen lakes in winter and stored them in underground ice houses for use in summer, but the idea of shipping ice to hot countries thousands of kilometres away seemed absurd. The man who proved otherwise was Frederic Tudor, the son of a wealthy Boston family, who became convinced that there was money to be made by selling the ice of New England's frozen ponds to the inhabitants of the Caribbean. Tudor's first attempt, in 1806, was a commercial disaster. He bought a ship, filled it with ice and sent it to the island of Martinique. Much of the cargo survived the voyage, but there was nowhere on the island to store it, and local people had no idea what to do with it. The ice melted within weeks, and Tudor lost a great deal of money. Over the following years, further losses, combined with a fall in trade caused by political conflict, left him deeply in debt, and at one point he was briefly imprisoned for failing to pay what he owed. Tudor, however, refused to give up, and he gradually solved the problems that had defeated him. He experimented with different materials for insulating ice and found that sawdust, which was produced in huge quantities by the timber mills of Maine and could be obtained almost free of charge, was one of the most effective. He built ice houses in the ports he supplied, so that the ice could be stored after it arrived. Just as importantly, he worked to create demand. He persuaded bar owners to serve cold drinks at the same price as warm ones, reasoning that once customers had tasted them, they would not want to go back, and he showed hospitals how ice could be used to treat patients with fevers. The business was transformed in the 1820s by a new method of harvesting. One of Tudor's suppliers, Nathaniel Wyeth, invented a horse-drawn cutter that cut deep parallel grooves into the surface of a frozen pond. The ice could then be split into blocks of identical size. Uniform blocks could be packed tightly together, which reduced melting, and they made it far easier to calculate the amount of ice in a cargo. Ice harvesting became a large seasonal industry, employing thousands of farm workers during the winter months, when there was little other work for them. Tudor's most remarkable achievement came in 1833, when he sent a shipment of around 180 tonnes of ice from Boston to Calcutta, in India, a voyage of about four months that crossed the equator twice. More than half of the cargo survived. The ice was received with astonishment, and the British residents of the city, who had previously relied on expensive methods of cooling drinks, quickly built a large ice house to store future shipments. Over the following decades, American ice was shipped to ports in South America, Asia and Australia, and by the time of Tudor's death in 1864 he had become extremely rich and was widely known as the 'Ice King'. The trade continued to grow after Tudor's death. Ice from New England, and later from Norway, which exported large quantities to Britain, was used not only to cool drinks but also to preserve food. Railway companies developed refrigerated wagons cooled by ice, which allowed meat from the American Midwest to be transported to the cities of the east coast. Ice became so important that a warm winter, which produced thin ice, could cause prices to rise sharply. Yet the natural ice trade was eventually overtaken by technology. READING PASSAGE 3 (Questions 27-40) You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27-40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below. Pen or Keyboard? Why Handwriting Still Matters In many classrooms today, children spend more time typing than writing by hand, and the change has prompted a lively debate. Some educators argue that handwriting, and joined-up or cursive writing in particular, is an outdated skill that takes up valuable lesson time. In 2016, Finland removed the requirement to teach cursive writing from its national curriculum and placed greater emphasis on typing. Other countries have moved in the opposite direction: several American states that had dropped cursive from their schools have since passed laws to bring it back. Who is right? In my view, the evidence suggests that handwriting is far from obsolete, although not every form of it deserves the same priority. Much of the most interesting research concerns young children who are learning to read. In one series of studies, children who had not yet learned to read were taught letters in one of three ways: by writing them freehand, by tracing them, or by typing them on a keyboard. When the children were later shown letters while their brain activity was recorded, those who had learned by freehand writing showed much stronger activity in the brain regions used for reading than those in the other two groups. The researchers suggested that the messy, variable shapes produced by a child's own hand help the brain to learn what makes a letter recognisable. Similar arguments are made about older children. In a study carried out in the United States, children aged between about seven and twelve were asked to write essays both by hand and on a keyboard. The younger children in particular wrote more words, wrote faster and expressed more ideas when they used a pen than when they typed. The study was relatively small, however, and children who had been taught keyboard skills from an early age might have performed quite differently. Later research has produced mixed results, and I think it is wise to treat findings of this kind with some caution. Even so, there are good reasons to think that handwriting engages the brain in useful ways. For most adults, writing by hand is slower than typing, and this slowness forces the writer to select and organise information rather than simply recording it. A recent study that recorded brain activity in young adults found that writing by hand produced more widespread connections between different brain regions than typing did, a pattern associated with memory and learning. None of this proves that handwriting makes people cleverer, but it does suggest that the physical act of forming letters engages the brain in ways that pressing keys does not. There are also practical reasons for teaching handwriting. Many examinations are still taken on paper, and students whose handwriting is slow or difficult to read may be unable to show what they know. Children who struggle to form letters often find writing so tiring that they write less, which in turn limits the development of their written expression. For these children, early and regular practice can make a considerable difference. Handwriting also remains common in everyday life, from filling in forms to writing quick notes and cards, and some people find that planning their ideas on paper helps them to think more freely than working on a screen. The case for cursive writing is less clear. Supporters claim that joined-up writing is faster and helps with spelling, and that people who cannot read cursive will be unable to read historical documents or letters from older relatives. These arguments are not without merit, but the evidence that cursive offers special benefits over clear printed writing is limited. What matters most, it seems to me, is that children can write legibly and fluently, whatever style they use. None of this means that typing should be neglected. Most adults now do the majority of their writing on screens, and keyboard skills are essential for work and study. The sensible approach is not to choose between the pen and the keyboard but to teach both, giving handwriting priority in the early years, when it appears to support reading and spelling, and introducing typing as children grow older. Above all, decisions about the curriculum should be guided by evidence, rather than by nostalgia for the past or by enthusiasm for the latest technology. prompt.en: 11-14 minutes · 3 parts Speaking test The Speaking test is a face-to-face interview with an examiner and is recorded. It lasts 11-14 minutes. A recording of the examiner's prompts with timed pauses is provided in audio/speaking_examiner_prompts.mp3 for self-practice; record yourself answering. Part 1: Introduction and interview (4-5 minutes) The examiner asks about familiar topics. Topic: Mornings • Are you a morning person? • What do you usually do first thing in the morning? • Has your morning routine changed since you were a child? • Do you prefer to study or work in the morning or in the evening? Topic: Sport • Do you play any sports? • What sports are popular in your country? • Did you do much sport at school? • Do you prefer watching sport or taking part? Part 2: Individual long turn (3-4 minutes, including 1 minute of preparation) Describe an occasion when you had to wait a long time for something. You should say: • what you were waiting for • how long you had to wait • what you did while you were waiting • and explain how you felt about the wait. You will have 1 minute to prepare and may make notes. Then speak for 1-2 minutes. The examiner may ask one brief follow-up question, e.g.: Are you generally a patient person? Part 3: Two-way discussion (4-5 minutes) Patience • Why do some people find it difficult to wait? • Do you think young people are less patient than older people? • In what situations is patience most important? The pace of modern life • Why does modern life seem to move so quickly nowadays? • What are the disadvantages of always wanting things immediately? • How could people slow down their lives? The Hat That Was Never From Panama Few items of clothing are as closely associated with a place as the Panama hat, the light, cream-coloured straw hat worn by everyone from colonial officials to film stars. Yet the name is one of history's great misunderstandings. The hats have never been made in Panama. For more than three centuries they have been woven by hand in Ecuador, a country several hundred kilometres to the south, and Ecuadorians are understandably keen to correct the error. The hats are made from the fibres of the toquilla plant, which looks like a palm but in fact belongs to a different plant family. It grows in the humid coastal lowlands of Ecuador. Young leaves are cut before they open, boiled to remove their green colour and then dried in the sun, where they curl into thin, round strands. Weaving begins at the centre of the crown and proceeds outwards in a spiral, with new strands added as the hat grows. The finest hats are woven so tightly that, according to a popular claim, they can hold water, although few owners have been willing to test this. The most celebrated hats come from the small coastal town of Montecristi. Here, weavers traditionally work in the early morning and late evening, when the air is cooler and more humid, because the fibres become brittle in the heat of the day. A hat of ordinary quality may be finished in a few days, but a top-grade Montecristi hat, with more than a thousand weaves in every square inch, can take a skilled weaver four or five months. Quality is judged by holding the hat up to the light and counting the rows, and by the evenness of the weave rather than its colour. Once the weaving is complete, the hat still passes through several further stages: the loose ends of straw are trimmed and tied off, the hat is washed and bleached, and it is beaten with a wooden mallet and ironed to soften the straw before being shaped into a particular style. Each of these stages is often carried out by a different specialist. The hats acquired their misleading name in the nineteenth century, when Ecuadorian merchants found it easier to sell their goods in Panama, which was then a busy crossing point between the Atlantic and Pacific oceans. Panama's ports offered regular shipping connections to North America, Europe and the west coast of South America, so traders there could reach a far larger market than in Ecuador itself. Sales rose dramatically after 1849, when thousands of gold prospectors travelled through Panama on their way to California and bought the hats to protect themselves from the tropical sun. Buyers in North America and Europe came to know them simply by the name of the place where they had been purchased. International fame arrived in 1906, when the American president Theodore Roosevelt visited the construction site of the Panama Canal. Photographs of the president in a white straw hat appeared in newspapers around the world, and demand soared. By the 1940s, hats were among Ecuador's most valuable exports, and tens of thousands of families in the coastal provinces and in the highland city of Cuenca depended on weaving for part of their income. The boom did not last. After the Second World War, hats in general went out of fashion, particularly among men, and exports fell sharply. Weaving communities faced a further challenge from cheap imitations, many of them made by machine from paper straw, which could be sold for a fraction of the price.
