Moving Stairs: The Escalator and the Modern City A The first moving staircase was designed to entertain rather than to transport. In 1896, an American inventor named Jesse Reno installed what he called an 'inclined elevator' on a pier at Coney Island, a seaside resort near New York. Passengers stood on a sloping belt that carried them about two metres upwards, and the ride was so popular that it is said to have carried tens of thousands of people in its first few weeks. A few years later, a rival design by Charles Seeberger, which had flat steps rather than a sloping belt, won a prize at the Paris Exhibition of 1900. Seeberger combined the Latin word 'scala', meaning steps, with the word 'elevator' to create the name 'escalator', which his company registered as a trademark. B Although escalators have changed in appearance since then, the basic mechanism remains much the same. Each step is attached to a pair of chains that form a continuous loop, driven by an electric motor at the top. Wheels on each step run along two tracks, and the tracks are shaped so that the steps form a staircase on the incline but flatten out at the top and bottom, allowing passengers to step on and off safely. The steps then turn upside down and return underneath. A moving handrail, driven by the same motor, travels at the same speed as the steps, while metal plates with teeth like a comb, known as comb plates, guide each step into the landing so that nothing can be trapped. C In busy places, escalators have a decisive advantage over lifts. A lift must stop, open its doors and wait for passengers, and people arriving in the meantime must queue. An escalator, by contrast, never stops, so passengers can board the moment they arrive. A single escalator can move several thousand people an hour, far more than a lift occupying the same space. This is why underground railway stations, airports and department stores, which must deal with sudden crowds, depend so heavily on them. In some cities, outdoor escalators have even been built to carry residents up steep hillsides that would otherwise be difficult to climb. Many escalators can also be reversed, running upwards during the morning rush and downwards in the evening, to match the direction in which most people are travelling. D In many countries, there is an unwritten rule that people who want to stand should keep to one side, leaving the other side free for those who want to walk. In 2015 and 2016, however, London Underground tested this custom at Holborn station, which has some of the longest escalators on the network. During the morning rush hour, staff asked passengers to stand on both sides. On a long escalator, it turned out, relatively few people choose to walk, so the walking side was often half-empty while long queues formed at the bottom for the standing side. When everyone stood, the number of people carried at peak times rose by around thirty per cent. Despite these results, the experiment was not extended, partly because changing such a deeply rooted habit proved extremely difficult. E Because escalators traditionally run all day whether or not anyone is using them, they can consume a great deal of electricity. Modern designs address this in several ways. Sensors detect when no passengers are approaching and slow the escalator down to a crawl, or stop it altogether, starting it again as soon as someone steps near. Some escalators that carry people downwards can even generate electricity, since the weight of the passengers helps to turn the motor, and this energy can be fed back into the building's power supply. The Case for Learning by Heart For much of history, learning by heart was at the centre of education. Children recited multiplication tables, poems, lists of rivers and the dates of kings, and the ability to repeat long passages from memory was regarded as a sign of a well-educated mind. Over the last century, however, memorisation has fallen out of favour. It is now commonly dismissed as 'rote learning', a mechanical activity that produces parrots rather than thinkers, and many teachers have been encouraged to replace it with activities that develop understanding and creativity. I believe that this rejection has gone too far, and that a certain amount of learning by heart deserves a place in every classroom. The most common objection is that memorisation is pointless when any fact can be found in seconds on a phone. This argument, it seems to me, misunderstands how thinking works. Psychologists distinguish between working memory, which holds the small amount of information we are actively thinking about, and long-term memory, which stores what we know. Working memory is severely limited; most people can hold only a handful of new items in mind at once. When the facts we need are already secure in long-term memory, they can be called up without effort, leaving working memory free for reasoning. A pupil who must stop to work out seven times eight has little capacity left for the problem that the calculation was meant to solve. The point is illustrated by a well-known series of studies of chess players. When experienced players were shown a position from a real game for a few seconds, they could reconstruct it almost perfectly, while beginners remembered only a few pieces. When the pieces were placed randomly, however, the experts did little better than the beginners. Their advantage lay not in a superior memory in general but in a vast store of familiar patterns, built up over years, which allowed them to see meaning where a novice saw only a jumble. Expertise in any field, I would argue, rests on a similar foundation of stored knowledge. None of this is to defend the dreary drills that critics rightly remember from their own schooldays. Memorising words without understanding them is of little value, and pupils who can recite a definition but cannot apply it have learned very little. The aim should be to commit to memory material that has already been understood, or that will be understood more fully as a result of being remembered. A poem learned by heart, for example, can be turned over in the mind long after the lesson has ended, and its meanings may only become clear years later. Research on memory also suggests that the methods used in many schools are inefficient. Reading notes again and again, which many students consider the best way to revise, produces a feeling of familiarity but relatively poor long-term retention. Far more effective is what psychologists call retrieval practice: trying to recall information without looking at it, for instance by answering questions or testing oneself with cards. Spreading this practice out over days and weeks, rather than cramming it into a single evening, improves retention still further. It also helps to mix different topics within a single session, so that learners must work out which knowledge is relevant to each question. Learning by heart, done well, is therefore not a matter of endless repetition but of regular, effortful recall. There are also less obvious benefits. Pupils who have learned a speech or a poem by heart often speak with greater confidence, because they have a stock of well-made sentences to draw on. Some teachers report that memorisation can be a source of pride for pupils who struggle in other areas of school, since it rewards effort rather than prior advantage. These claims are harder to measure, and I would not want to overstate them, but they are consistent with my own experience as a teacher. I am not suggesting that schools should return to the classrooms of a hundred years ago. Discussion, investigation and creative work all have an essential role to play. But understanding and memory are not opposites; each depends on the other. A curriculum that ignores memory in the name of understanding risks producing pupils who have been taught to think but have nothing to think about. Tulip Fever: The Story of a Flower and a Market Tulips are so closely associated with the Netherlands today that it is easy to forget they are not native to the country. Wild tulips grow in the mountains of Central Asia, and the flower was first cultivated in gardens in Persia and later in the Ottoman Empire, where it became a symbol of wealth and refinement. Tulip bulbs reached western Europe in the middle of the sixteenth century, probably as gifts from diplomats who had visited the Ottoman court in Constantinople. In the Netherlands, the key figure was a botanist named Carolus Clusius, who in 1593 became director of the new botanical garden at the University of Leiden. Clusius planted a collection of tulip bulbs and studied them carefully, but he was reluctant to share them, and asked very high prices from anyone who wished to buy. According to one account, some of his bulbs were stolen from the garden at night, and from these, tulips spread across the Dutch provinces. The most admired tulips of the period were not the plain red or yellow flowers common today but so-called 'broken' tulips, whose petals were marked with dramatic streaks and flames of a contrasting colour. Growers could not explain why a plain tulip would sometimes produce striped flowers, and the effect could not be reliably reproduced. We now know that the patterns were caused by a virus, carried from plant to plant by small insects called aphids. The virus also weakened the bulbs, so the most beautiful varieties reproduced slowly, which made them rare and expensive. One particularly prized variety, the Viceroy, had purple flames on a white background. The Dutch Republic in the early seventeenth century was one of the richest societies in Europe, and a growing class of merchants and craftsmen had money to spend. Tulips became fashionable, and their price began to rise. Because tulips flower only briefly in spring, and bulbs can only be safely lifted from the ground in summer, most trading took place during the rest of the year in the form of contracts: a buyer agreed to pay a certain price for a bulb that would be delivered when it was dug up. Contracts were frequently resold several times before the bulbs were delivered, so that a single bulb might change hands many times on paper while it remained in the ground. Most traders never intended to plant the bulbs at all; they hoped only to sell the contract on at a higher price. Much of this trading took place not in formal markets but in the back rooms of taverns. In the winter of 1636 to 1637, prices rose to extraordinary levels. A single bulb of the most famous variety, the red-and-white Semper Augustus, was reportedly offered for a sum that could have bought a fine house in Amsterdam. Then, in February 1637, at an auction in the city of Haarlem, buyers suddenly failed to appear. Within days, prices collapsed throughout the country, and many people found themselves bound by contracts to pay far more for bulbs than the bulbs were now worth. For a long time, this episode was told as a story of national madness, in which ordinary people sold their homes and businesses to buy bulbs and were ruined when the market crashed. Much of this picture comes from a popular book published by the Scottish writer Charles Mackay in 1841, nearly two centuries after the events. Mackay relied heavily on pamphlets written at the time by moralists who disapproved of the trade and had every reason to exaggerate its excesses. Finding the Way Home: The Mystery of the Homing Pigeon A For thousands of years, people have taken advantage of the pigeon's remarkable ability to return to its home loft after being released far away. Pigeons carried messages in ancient Egypt and Persia, and in 1850 the news agency founded by Paul Julius Reuter used them to fly stock-market prices between the German city of Aachen and Brussels, filling a gap in the telegraph line. During the siege of Paris in 1870 and 1871, pigeons carried thousands of messages into the surrounded city, photographed in tiny print and rolled into tubes attached to their tail feathers. During the First World War, a pigeon named Cher Ami delivered a message that helped to save almost two hundred trapped American soldiers, and was awarded a French medal for bravery. Even today, pigeon racing remains a popular sport, with birds regularly returning from distances of several hundred kilometres in a single day. B How pigeons manage this has puzzled scientists for more than a century. Navigation requires two separate abilities, which researchers often compare to a map and a compass. A compass alone is not enough: a bird that knows which direction is north still needs to know where it is in relation to home before it can choose the right direction to fly. Most research has therefore tried to identify the information that pigeons use for each of these two tasks, and a number of possible sources have been proposed. Some birds may rely on several different sources at once, switching between them as conditions change. C The best-established compass is the sun. Because the sun's position changes during the day, a bird using it to find direction must take the time of day into account. In the northern hemisphere, a pigeon released at noon that wishes to fly south must head roughly towards the sun, while at six in the morning the sun lies far to the east, so the bird must fly at a very different angle to it. Researchers tested this by keeping pigeons in a room where the lights were switched on and off six hours later than the real sunrise and sunset. When released, the birds flew off in a direction that was wrong by roughly ninety degrees, exactly as would be expected if their internal clock had been shifted and they were relying on the sun. D On cloudy days, however, pigeons can still find their way, which suggests that they have a second compass. In the 1970s, a researcher attached small magnets to the backs of pigeons' heads. On sunny days, the magnets made no difference, but on overcast days, the birds became disoriented. Tiny particles of an iron-rich mineral have since been found in pigeons' beaks, and for some years these were thought to be the magnetic sensor. Later work showed that the particles belonged to immune cells, and the exact location of the magnetic sense remains uncertain. E The 'map' sense has proved even harder to explain. One controversial theory, developed largely by Italian scientists, holds that pigeons learn the smells carried by the winds that blow over their home loft and use these to work out their position. Pigeons whose sense of smell has been blocked often have difficulty returning from unfamiliar places. Another theory suggests that pigeons can hear extremely low-frequency sounds, known as infrasound, produced by ocean waves and by the shape of the land, and that these sounds act as a kind of acoustic map. Supporters of this theory point to occasions when large numbers of racing pigeons have become lost on the same day, which they link to unusual atmospheric conditions. Tidiness: An Overrated Virtue? In recent years, tidiness has acquired an almost moral significance. Bestselling books promise that clearing out our cupboards will transform our lives; television programmes show families weeping with relief as their possessions are carried away; and social media is full of photographs of spotless kitchens and perfectly organised drawers. The message is clear: a cluttered home reflects a cluttered mind, and order is the route to happiness. Entire businesses now exist to help people sort, store and discard their belongings. I want to suggest that this message, while not entirely wrong, is considerably exaggerated, and that a little mess deserves a better reputation. Let me begin with what the research does show. In one widely reported study, people were asked to describe their homes, and those who used words such as 'cluttered' and 'unfinished' were found to have higher levels of a stress hormone over the course of the day, and their mood tended to worsen as the evening went on. It would be foolish to dismiss such findings. For some people, a home overflowing with unused objects is a genuine source of anxiety, and for a small number, the inability to throw anything away is a serious psychological condition that requires professional help. But it is a large step from these findings to the claim that everyone should aim for minimalism. The study I have just described was relatively small, and it measured how people felt about their homes rather than how untidy the homes actually were. It is quite possible that people who are already stressed are more likely to notice, and to resent, the mess around them. Untidiness may be a symptom of a busy life rather than its cause. There is also evidence that disorder can have benefits. In a series of experiments at an American university, participants were placed either in a neat office or in one with papers and books scattered about. Those in the tidy room were more likely to choose a healthy snack and to make a donation to charity, which suggests that order encourages conventional, well-behaved choices. However, when asked to think of new uses for an everyday object, the participants in the messy room produced ideas that independent judges rated as more creative. Disorder, the researchers suggested, may encourage people to break away from convention. The researchers were careful to point out that neither kind of room was better overall; each simply encouraged a different way of thinking. Anyone who has worked in an office will also recognise that the person with the untidiest desk is not necessarily the least organised. Researchers who study how people manage information distinguish between 'filers', who put documents away in a system of folders, and 'pilers', who leave them in heaps on their desks. Pilers are often criticised, yet their piles are frequently arranged by an informal logic: the documents they are working on are near the top, and those that are no longer needed gradually sink to the bottom. Filers, by contrast, sometimes store documents so carefully that they forget they have them. Indeed, some pilers argue that putting a document out of sight is the surest way to forget about it. Finally, there is the question of time. Keeping a home or an office in perfect order requires constant effort, and the hours spent tidying, sorting and labelling are hours not spent with friends, on hobbies or simply resting. It is worth asking how many of those hours are really necessary, and whose standards they are meant to satisfy. For many families with young children, a perfectly tidy house is an unrealistic goal, and the pressure to achieve it can itself become a source of guilt and conflict. None of this is an argument for squalor. Dirty dishes, lost bills and floors that cannot be crossed without danger are nobody's idea of a good life. But between the show home and the rubbish tip there is a wide range of acceptable conditions, and where each person feels comfortable within that range is largely a matter of temperament. Instead of treating tidiness as a virtue and mess as a failing, we might simply accept that people differ, and that a desk covered in papers may belong to someone who knows exactly where everything is. prompt.en: 11-14 minutes · 3 parts Speaking test The Speaking test is a face-to-face interview with an examiner and is recorded. It lasts 11-14 minutes. A recording of the examiner's prompts with timed pauses is provided in audio/speaking_examiner_prompts.mp3 for self-practice; record yourself answering. Part 1: Introduction and interview (4-5 minutes) The examiner asks about familiar topics. Topic: Losing things • Do you often lose things? • What do you do to avoid losing important items? • Have you ever lost something valuable? • How do you feel when you can't find something? Topic: Public parks • Is there a park near where you live? • What do people usually do in parks in your town? • Did you spend much time in parks as a child? • Should your town have more parks? Part 2: Individual long turn (3-4 minutes, including 1 minute of preparation) Describe something your family has kept for a long time. You should say: • what the object is • how long your family has had it • where it is kept • and explain why your family has kept this object. You will have 1 minute to prepare and may make notes. Then speak for 1-2 minutes. The examiner may ask one brief follow-up question, e.g.: Will you keep this object yourself one day? Part 3: Two-way discussion (4-5 minutes) Family possessions • Thinking of families you know, what kinds of objects get passed down to children? • Are such objects more important for older people than for younger people? • How has the internet changed the way families keep memories? Antiques and the past • What makes some people interested in collecting antiques? • Should museums display ordinary household objects as well as valuable ones? • How can old objects help young people understand history? END OF TEST

prompt.en: 60 minutes · 3 passages · 40 questions Read the three passages and answer Questions 1-40. You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Transfer time is NOT added at the end of the Reading test. READING PASSAGE 1 (Questions 1-13) You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1-13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below. Teeth That Lock: The Long Road to the Zip Fastener Few inventions are used as often, or noticed as rarely, as the zip. It holds together jackets, bags, tents and boots all over the world, and billions are produced every year. Yet the device took several decades to perfect, and for much of that time it seemed unlikely ever to become a commercial success. The first serious attempt was made by an American engineer named Whitcomb Judson, who in 1893 patented what he called a 'clasp locker'. According to a story told later by his company, Judson was motivated by a friend who suffered from a bad back and found it painful to bend down to fasten the long rows of buttons and hooks on his boots, which were then standard. Whether or not this story is true, Judson's device was intended above all for footwear. It consisted of a series of hooks and eyes that were joined together by a sliding mechanism. Judson, who had already patented several devices for street railways, saw the fastener as one more mechanical problem waiting to be solved. Judson exhibited his invention at the World's Fair in Chicago in 1893, but it attracted little attention. The clasp locker was expensive to make by hand, and it had a serious weakness: it tended to spring open unexpectedly, which, in clothing, could be extremely embarrassing. Judson and his business partners founded a company to manufacture an improved version, but sales remained disappointing for years, and the company came close to collapse. A second version, intended to be easier to produce by machine, proved even less reliable, and one early customer reportedly returned an entire order of fasteners because they would not stay closed. The breakthrough came from a Swedish-born engineer, Gideon Sundback, who joined the company in 1906. Sundback is said to have worked on the problem with particular determination after the death of his wife in 1911. Sundback abandoned the hook-and-eye design altogether. In 1913 he developed a fastener in which two rows of small, identical metal teeth were drawn together by a slider, each tooth fitting into a hollow in the back of the one opposite. This 'hookless fastener', as it was called, was far more secure than earlier versions. Equally important, Sundback designed a machine that could produce the fastener cheaply and in large quantities, cutting the metal teeth and fixing them to a cloth tape in a single process. Even so, it was not clothing manufacturers who first took up the new device. Early customers used it for money belts and tobacco pouches, and the United States military bought large numbers for flying suits during the First World War. In 1923, the rubber company B.F. Goodrich used the fasteners on a new line of rubber boots, and gave them a memorable name, taken from the sound the slider made: the 'zipper'. The company registered the name as a trademark for its boots, but the word soon came to be used for the fastener itself. Acceptance in fashion was slow. Many tailors regarded the zip as a cheap, mechanical substitute for buttons, and there were concerns that it might rust or break. In the 1930s, however, manufacturers of children's clothing began to promote zips as a way of helping children to dress themselves, and some leading fashion designers used them boldly in evening wear. A decisive moment came when zips started to replace buttons on men's trousers, a change that was promoted heavily in magazine advertisements. Trousers with zips were advertised as a way of avoiding the embarrassment of a forgotten button, and by the end of the decade the debate was largely over. Small Talk, Big Rewards Few social activities have a worse reputation than small talk. Conversations about the weather, the traffic or the weekend are widely regarded as a tedious ritual, something to be endured at parties and in lifts until a more meaningful topic can be found. Many people say that they dislike it, and some popular writers on personality have argued that it is particularly exhausting for introverts. I want to argue that small talk is more valuable than its reputation suggests, and that we would all benefit from doing a little more of it. Consider first the evidence from research on everyday encounters. In one well-known series of experiments, commuters on trains and buses in an American city were asked either to start a conversation with a stranger, to sit in silence, or to behave as they normally would. Before the journey, most participants predicted that talking to a stranger would be the least pleasant option. In fact, those who talked reported the most enjoyable journeys, and none of them reported being rejected. Even participants who described themselves as shy enjoyed the conversations more than they had expected. The researchers concluded that people systematically underestimate how much others will want to talk to them, and how much they themselves will enjoy it. Other studies point in the same direction. Customers who exchanged a few friendly words with a barista when buying coffee reported a greater sense of belonging than those who kept the transaction as brief as possible. People who interact with a wider range of acquaintances during the day, from neighbours to shop assistants, tend to report better moods on those days, even when the interactions are very short. These relationships, which sociologists sometimes call 'weak ties', appear to contribute more to our wellbeing than we tend to assume. In another experiment, passers-by who were ignored by a stranger felt less connected to others than those who received a brief smile. Admittedly, one widely reported study seemed to suggest the opposite. Researchers who recorded fragments of participants' daily conversations found that the happiest people spent less time in small talk and more time in deeper, more substantive conversations. This finding is often quoted as evidence that small talk is worthless. But later attempts to repeat the study with larger groups found that the link between small talk and unhappiness largely disappeared. Substantive conversation does seem to be good for us, but that does not mean small talk is bad. Indeed, small talk is often the route by which deeper conversations begin. Very few friendships start with a discussion of the meaning of life; they start with a remark about the weather or a question about where someone bought their coat. Small talk allows people to signal goodwill, to judge whether the other person is interested in talking, and to discover shared interests at little risk. Small talk also follows predictable patterns, which is precisely why it feels safe: both people know roughly what is expected of them. Without it, the step to more meaningful conversation would be far more difficult. There are practical benefits too. In the workplace, brief informal conversations help colleagues to build trust, and people who know a little about each other's lives are more likely to cooperate and to ask for help when they need it. New employees, in particular, often learn the unwritten rules of an organisation through casual conversations in corridors and kitchens. Some organisations that moved entirely to online communication have found it necessary to create virtual spaces for casual chat, because the absence of such conversations was making teams less effective. None of this means that everyone must become a tireless conversationalist. People differ in how much social contact they want, and there are moments when a stranger plainly prefers to be left alone. But the evidence suggests that most of us are too pessimistic about how our attempts at conversation will be received. The next time you find yourself standing silently beside someone in a queue, it may be worth remembering that a few words about the weather could brighten both of your days. If the other person seems unwilling, the cost is a moment of mild awkwardness; if not, the reward may be a pleasant conversation or even a new friend. options.en: Buy something to eat Read an Academic Passage Read the passage and answer the questions. The Spread of Paper For centuries, writers in ancient China recorded texts on strips of bamboo tied together with cord, or on silk. Bamboo was cheap but heavy and bulky: a single long work could fill a cart. Silk was light and smooth but far too expensive for everyday use. According to tradition, a court official named Cai Lun invented paper in 105 CE by pounding tree bark, hemp, old rags, and fishing nets into a pulp, spreading it thin, and letting it dry. Archaeologists, however, have found fragments of paper that are considerably older than Cai Lun's time. Most historians now believe that Cai Lun refined an existing technique and promoted it at court, making paper more practical to produce. Over the following centuries, papermaking spread across East Asia. It reached the Islamic world in the eighth century; one well-known account links its arrival in the city of Samarkand to Chinese papermakers captured after a battle in 751. Paper mills soon operated in Baghdad and other cities, and the technique eventually reached Europe, where paper was being produced in Spain by the twelfth century.

The Dust Bowl During the 1930s, a series of severe droughts struck the southern Great Plains of the United States. Without rain, crops failed, and strong winds lifted the dry topsoil into enormous dust storms. Some storms, known as 'black blizzards', darkened the sky at midday and carried dust hundreds of kilometers to the east. The droughts alone did not cause the disaster. In the preceding decades, high wheat prices and new machinery such as tractors had encouraged farmers to plow millions of acres of native prairie grass. Those grasses had deep roots that held the soil in place and retained moisture. Once they were removed, the exposed soil was easily blown away, and the drought exacerbated a problem that farming practices had created. The federal government responded with new programs. In 1935, it established the Soil Conservation Service, which taught farmers techniques such as contour plowing, crop rotation, and planting rows of trees as windbreaks. These methods reduced erosion significantly, and when rain finally returned in the late 1930s, the region gradually recovered, though many families had already left in search of work elsewhere.

Dr. Patel: Many cities around the world have started to close parts of their downtown areas to private cars, turning streets into spaces for pedestrians, cyclists, and public transportation. Supporters say this makes city centers cleaner and more pleasant; critics argue that it hurts local businesses and makes the city harder to reach for some people. What do you think? Should cities ban private cars from their downtown areas? Why or why not? Kenji: I think cities should definitely do this. Car-free streets reduce air pollution and noise, and they are much safer for pedestrians. When I visited a city with a car-free center, the streets were full of people walking, eating outside, and shopping. It felt more like a community. Laura: I disagree. Not everyone can walk or cycle easily. Older people, people with disabilities, and families with small children often depend on cars. options.en: Call the airport for information Read an Academic Passage Read the passage and answer the questions. Seeing with Sound Most bats hunt at night, when their eyes are of limited use. Instead, many species rely on echolocation. A bat produces a series of very high-pitched calls, usually far above the range of human hearing, and listens for the echoes that bounce back from objects around it. By comparing the timing and strength of these echoes, the bat builds a detailed picture of its surroundings. Echolocation is remarkably precise. Some bats can detect a wire thinner than a human hair, and many can judge not only the distance to an insect but also its size and the direction in which it is moving. As a bat closes in on its prey, it calls more and more rapidly, producing a final 'buzz' of up to two hundred calls per second just before the catch. Insects have not been passive victims. Some moths have evolved ears that are sensitive to bat calls; when they hear one, they fold their wings and drop toward the ground. Others produce clicking sounds of their own, which may warn bats that they taste unpleasant or interfere with the bats' ability to process echoes.

options.en: The shopper should visit the Town Square market. Read an Academic Passage Read the passage and answer the questions. The Coffeehouses of London Coffee arrived in England in the mid-seventeenth century, and the first London coffeehouse opened in 1652. Within a few decades, the city had hundreds of them. For the price of a single cup, customers could stay for hours, reading newspapers and joining conversations with strangers. Coffeehouses quickly became centers of information. Newspapers and pamphlets were left on the tables, and news from ships and foreign cities often reached coffeehouses before it reached anyone else. Because people of different social ranks sat at the same tables, the coffeehouses were sometimes called 'penny universities': for the cost of a penny, anyone could listen to discussions of politics, science, and trade. Some coffeehouses became associated with particular activities. Merchants and ship owners gathered at Edward Lloyd's coffeehouse to exchange shipping news, and this gathering eventually developed into Lloyd's of London, one of the world's best-known insurance markets. Not everyone approved of these lively spaces, however. In 1675, King Charles II tried to close them, fearing that they encouraged criticism of the government. The order caused such protest that it was withdrawn within days.

Some people believe these requirements produce well-rounded graduates. Others feel they waste time and money that students could spend on their main field. What do you think? The Monarch Migration Each autumn, millions of monarch butterflies leave the northern United States and southern Canada and fly south, some traveling more than 4,000 kilometers. Most of the eastern population spends the winter in a small area of mountain forest in central Mexico, where the butterflies cluster so densely on fir trees that branches bend under their weight. What makes this journey remarkable is that no individual butterfly makes the round trip. The monarchs that fly south in autumn live for up to eight months, far longer than summer generations, which live only a few weeks. In spring, they begin flying north and lay eggs along the way. It takes three or four generations to reach the northern breeding grounds, so the butterflies that arrive in Mexico the following autumn have never been there before. Researchers have found that monarchs navigate partly by using the position of the sun, combined with an internal clock located in their antennae. Experiments suggest that they may also sense Earth's magnetic field, which could help them on cloudy days. How they find the same few mountain forests each year, however, remains uncertain.

The Inca Road System At its height in the early sixteenth century, the Inca Empire stretched more than 4,000 kilometers along the western side of South America. Holding together such a vast territory, much of it in the high Andes mountains, required an extraordinary network of roads. The Inca road system, known as the Qhapaq Nan, eventually covered roughly 40,000 kilometers. The Inca did not use wheeled vehicles or horses, so their roads were designed for people on foot and for herds of llamas carrying goods. Where the terrain was steep, builders cut stone staircases into the mountainside. To cross deep river gorges, communities wove suspension bridges from grass rope, which had to be rebuilt regularly. One such bridge, at Q'eswachaka in Peru, is still rebuilt by local villagers every year. Along the roads, the state built thousands of way stations where travelers could rest and find supplies. The Value of Salt Today salt is one of the cheapest items in any grocery store, but for most of human history it was a valuable commodity. Humans and their animals need salt to survive, and before refrigeration, salt was also the most important way to preserve food. Meat and fish packed in salt could be stored for months and transported over long distances. Because salt was so essential, its production and trade were often controlled by governments. In ancient China, the state held a monopoly on salt for long periods, and salt taxes provided a large share of government income. In parts of West Africa, salt from the Sahara was carried south by camel caravans and was sometimes traded for gold. Salt has also left its mark on language. The English word 'salary' is often said to come from a Roman practice of paying soldiers in salt, although historians point out that there is little direct evidence for this story. What is certain is that the Latin word for salt, sal, is the origin of words such as 'salad', from the Roman habit of salting vegetables.

Tsunamis A tsunami is a series of ocean waves caused by a sudden, large movement of water, most often an undersea earthquake. When part of the sea floor suddenly rises or drops, the entire column of water above it moves, and waves spread outward in all directions. In the deep ocean, a tsunami may be less than a meter high and can pass beneath a ship almost unnoticed. However, it travels at tremendous speed, sometimes more than 700 kilometers per hour, about as fast as a jet airplane. As the waves approach the shore and the water becomes shallower, they slow down, and their energy is compressed into a much smaller volume of water. As a result, they grow dramatically in height. One of the warning signs of an approaching tsunami is a sudden retreat of the sea, which can expose large areas of the sea floor. Some people have been drawn out to look, not realizing the danger. Today, networks of sensors on the ocean floor detect changes in water pressure and send alerts, giving coastal communities time to move to higher ground.

prompt.en: 12. Write for an Academic Discussion (10 minutes) Your professor is teaching a class on sociology. Write a post responding to the professor's question. In your response, you should do the following: • Express and support your opinion. • Make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words. Dr. Evans: More and more young adults are choosing to live with their parents into their late twenties, often to save money. Some people see this as a sensible financial decision. Others believe that living independently is an important part of becoming an adult and that staying at home delays this. What is your opinion? Is it a good idea for young adults to live with their parents after finishing their education? Why or why not? Hana: I think it's a smart choice. Rents are very high, and living at home lets young people save for a deposit on their own place or pay off student loans. In many cultures, it's completely normal for several generations to live together. Marcus: I understand the financial reasons, but I think people learn a lot from living on their own: budgeting, cooking, solving problems without help. options.en: He works at the student center. Read an Academic Passage Read the passage and answer the questions. The Origins of Writing Writing was invented independently in several parts of the world, but the earliest known system developed in Mesopotamia, in what is now Iraq, more than five thousand years ago. Surprisingly, it was not created to record stories or laws. The first written records were accounts: lists of goods such as grain, sheep, and beer that were collected, stored, and distributed by temple officials. These early records used simple pictures pressed into tablets of wet clay. Over time, scribes began making the signs with the cut end of a reed, which left wedge-shaped marks. This style of writing is known as cuneiform, from the Latin word for 'wedge'. The pictures gradually became more abstract, and scribes began to use some signs for their sounds rather than their meanings, which allowed them to write names and, eventually, complete sentences. Once writing could represent spoken language, its uses multiplied. Cuneiform was used for letters, contracts, laws, and literature, including one of the oldest surviving epic poems. Learning it, however, took years of training, and only a small group of professional scribes could read and write. The system remained in use for about three thousand years before it was gradually replaced by alphabets, which needed far fewer signs.

options.en: The student should take yoga first. Read an Academic Passage Read the passage and answer the questions. Ocean Currents and Climate The oceans are constantly moving. At the surface, winds push the water into great currents that flow for thousands of kilometers. One of the best known is the Gulf Stream, which carries warm water from the Gulf of Mexico northward along the coast of North America and then across the Atlantic toward Europe. Along the way, it releases heat into the atmosphere. This heat helps explain why parts of northwestern Europe have relatively mild winters. Places in Britain and Norway, for example, are generally much warmer in winter than places at similar latitudes in eastern Canada, although scientists point out that winds and the shape of the continents also contribute to the difference. Deep below the surface, currents are driven not by wind but by differences in temperature and saltiness. In the far North Atlantic, surface water becomes very cold and salty, which makes it dense, so it sinks and flows slowly southward along the ocean floor. Water moving through this global system may take around a thousand years to complete a full circuit. Some scientists are concerned that melting ice could add so much fresh water to the North Atlantic that the sinking slows, which could change weather patterns on both sides of the ocean.

Dr. Okonkwo: Some universities are replacing traditional final exams with projects, such as research reports, presentations, or portfolios of work completed during the semester. Supporters say projects measure deeper understanding; critics say exams are fairer and better at checking what each student knows. Which do you think is the better way to assess students, and why? Leila: I prefer projects. In an exam, you just memorize facts for a few hours and forget them a week later. When I did a research project for my history class, I learned how to find sources and build an argument, which is much more useful. Owen: I see the benefits of projects, but they can be unfair. In group projects, some students do all the work, and others get the same grade. options.en: His laptop Read an Academic Passage Read the passage and answer the questions. Flattening the Globe: The Mercator Projection Any flat map of the world is a compromise. Earth is round, and it is impossible to flatten the surface of a sphere without stretching or tearing it somewhere. Mapmakers use mathematical methods called projections to transfer the globe onto paper, and every projection distorts something: shapes, sizes, distances, or directions. One of the most famous projections was published in 1569 by the Flemish mapmaker Gerardus Mercator. His map was designed for sailors. On it, a line of constant compass direction appears as a straight line, so a navigator could draw a course between two ports with a ruler and follow a single compass bearing. To achieve this, Mercator had to stretch the map more and more toward the poles. The result is that areas far from the equator appear much larger than they really are. Greenland, for example, looks about as large as Africa on a Mercator map, although Africa is roughly fourteen times bigger. Because the projection was used for centuries on classroom walls, critics argue that it has given many people a distorted picture of the world. Today, many atlases use other projections for general maps, though Mercator's design is still used for navigation and for many online street maps.

The Towns of Prairie Dogs Prairie dogs are not dogs at all but burrowing rodents related to squirrels. They live on the grasslands of western North America in large colonies known as towns. Some towns once covered hundreds of square kilometers and contained millions of animals. Each town is divided into small family groups called coteries, which defend their own section of the burrow system. Prairie dogs have a complex system of alarm calls. Researchers who recorded these calls found that they vary depending on the type of predator. A call warning of a hawk, for example, sounds different from one warning of a coyote, and the animals respond differently: they dive into their burrows when a hawk is announced but stand upright and watch when a coyote approaches. Some studies suggest that the calls even contain information about a predator's size and color. Prairie dogs are also important to the grassland ecosystem. The Harlem Renaissance In the early twentieth century, hundreds of thousands of African Americans moved from the rural South to cities in the North, a movement known as the Great Migration. Many settled in Harlem, a neighborhood in New York City. By the 1920s, Harlem had become the center of a remarkable burst of creativity in literature, music, and art that later became known as the Harlem Renaissance. Writers of the movement explored Black identity and everyday life with new pride and honesty. The poet Langston Hughes wrote about ordinary working people and used the rhythms of blues and jazz in his poems. In 1925, the philosopher Alain Locke published an influential collection of writing called The New Negro, which argued that Black artists could change how the nation saw African Americans. At the same time, jazz musicians such as Duke Ellington performed in Harlem's famous clubs, attracting large audiences. The Great Depression, which began in 1929, brought hard times to Harlem, and by the mid-1930s the movement had faded. Its influence, however, lasted much longer. The writers and musicians of the Harlem Renaissance inspired later generations of artists and helped prepare the ground for the civil rights movement.

The Paintings of Lascaux In 1940, four teenagers exploring a hillside in southwestern France found a narrow opening that led into a cave. Inside, they discovered walls covered with paintings of animals. The cave, called Lascaux, contains around six hundred paintings and about fifteen hundred engravings, and scientists estimate that they were made roughly seventeen thousand years ago. The most common subjects are horses, but the walls also show deer, bison, and large wild cattle called aurochs. The artists made their paints from minerals: red and yellow came from iron-rich earth, and black came from manganese and charcoal. They applied the paint with brushes, pads of moss or fur, and possibly by blowing it through hollow bones. Many of the images were painted high on the walls and ceilings, which suggests that the artists built some kind of scaffolding to reach them. After the cave opened to the public in 1948, more than a thousand visitors a day came to see it. Unfortunately, the carbon dioxide and moisture from their breath began to damage the paintings, and green growths appeared on the walls. In 1963, the cave was closed to the public. Twenty years later, an exact copy of part of the cave, called Lascaux II, was opened nearby so that visitors could still experience the art without harming the original.

The Story of the Ukulele The ukulele is a small, four-stringed instrument closely associated with Hawaii, but its origins lie thousands of kilometers away. In 1879, a ship arrived in Honolulu carrying hundreds of workers from the Portuguese island of Madeira, who had come to work on Hawaii's sugar plantations. Among them were several skilled woodworkers who brought with them a small guitar-like instrument called the machete. Soon after arriving, these craftsmen opened shops in Honolulu and began making instruments for local customers. Hawaiians quickly adopted the instrument and changed it to suit their own music. Makers began using koa, a wood that grows only in Hawaii and produces a warm, bright sound. The new instrument was named the ukulele, a Hawaiian word that is often translated as 'jumping flea,' perhaps because of the quick movement of a player's fingers. King Kalakaua, who ruled Hawaii at the time, was an enthusiastic supporter of traditional music and dance, and he featured the ukulele at royal events, which greatly increased its popularity. The ukulele became famous in the mainland United States after 1915, when Hawaiian musicians performed at a large international exhibition in San Francisco. Millions of visitors heard the instrument for the first time, and sales soared. Because ukuleles were inexpensive and relatively easy to learn, they became popular with amateur musicians. After a period of decline, the instrument has enjoyed a strong revival in recent decades, partly thanks to online videos in which performers share songs and lessons.

The Rise of Impressionism In nineteenth-century France, the most important place for an artist to show work was the official Salon, a huge annual exhibition in Paris. Its judges preferred carefully finished paintings of historical, religious, or mythological scenes, with smooth surfaces and invisible brushstrokes. Many young painters found these rules restrictive, and in 1863 so many works were rejected that the emperor allowed a separate exhibition for them, which became known as the Salon of the Rejected. In 1874, a group of these independent artists, including Camille Pissarro, Edgar Degas, and Berthe Morisot, organized their own exhibition. One critic mocked a painting in the show titled Impression, Sunrise, calling the whole group 'Impressionists.' The artists adopted the name. Rather than historical scenes, they painted modern life: city streets, cafés, train stations, and people relaxing in the countryside. They often worked outdoors, using quick, visible brushstrokes to capture the changing effects of light. Two inventions helped make this approach possible. Paint sold in metal tubes, available from the 1840s, allowed artists to carry their colors outside easily. New railway lines made it simple to travel from Paris to the coast or the countryside in a few hours. Although the Impressionists were often criticized at first, collectors gradually began buying their work, and by the end of the century their style had influenced painters around the world.

The Mountain Rice Terraces of the Philippines In the Cordillera mountains of northern Luzon, in the Philippines, steep slopes are covered with thousands of narrow, flat fields that rise like giant staircases. These rice terraces were built by the Ifugao people, and many of them are believed to be several hundred years old. In some places, the terraces climb more than a thousand meters up the mountainsides, and in 1995 a group of them was added to the list of World Heritage Sites. Growing rice on a mountain requires careful control of water. The Ifugao built the terraces with stone or earth walls and leveled each field so that it could hold a shallow pool of water. Water from streams and forests higher up the mountain is guided through a system of channels and bamboo pipes, flowing from one terrace to the next. Because the forests above the fields store rainwater and release it slowly, protecting these woodlands has always been part of farming the terraces. Today the terraces face serious threats. Many young people have moved to cities for work, leaving fewer farmers to repair walls and clear channels. When a wall collapses and is not repaired, water escapes and nearby fields can be damaged as well. Local organizations now run programs that teach traditional building methods to students and that encourage tourists to visit, hoping that new income will give young people a reason to stay.

The Dunning-Kruger Effect In 1999, the psychologists David Dunning and Justin Kruger published a study with a surprising finding. They gave university students tests of logical reasoning, grammar, and humor, and then asked each student to estimate how well they had done compared with others. Students who scored in the bottom quarter believed, on average, that they had performed better than most of their classmates. Their estimates were far higher than their actual results. Dunning and Kruger offered an explanation for this pattern. The skills needed to perform well in an area are often the same skills needed to judge performance in that area. A person who does not know the rules of grammar, for example, cannot easily recognize the mistakes in his own writing. In other words, people with little skill suffer twice: they make errors, and they are unable to see that they are making them. The researchers also found that the problem could be reduced. When low-scoring students were given a short lesson in the skill being tested, they became much better at judging their earlier performance and lowered their estimates. Interestingly, the highest-scoring students showed the opposite tendency: they slightly underestimated how well they had done, apparently because they assumed that tasks easy for them were also easy for everyone else.

The Way of Tea Tea arrived in Japan from China more than a thousand years ago, first as a medicine and later as a drink enjoyed by Buddhist monks, who used it to stay awake during long hours of meditation. Over several centuries, preparing and serving tea developed into a formal ceremony known as chanoyu, which means 'hot water for tea.' The ceremony uses matcha, a fine green powder that is whisked with hot water in a bowl rather than steeped in a pot. The tea master most responsible for shaping the ceremony was Sen no Rikyu, who lived in the sixteenth century. Rikyu rejected the fashion among wealthy lords for displaying expensive Chinese tea bowls and elaborate decorations. Instead, he favored simple, rough pottery and small, plain tea rooms, some with an entrance so low that guests had to bow and crawl inside. This, he believed, reminded everyone, whatever their rank, that they were equal inside the tea room. Every movement in the ceremony follows a set pattern, from the way the host cleans each utensil to the way guests turn the bowl before drinking. To an outsider, these rules may seem strict, but practitioners say they free the mind from everyday concerns and allow host and guests to focus completely on the present moment. Today, many Japanese people study the tea ceremony for years, and schools founded by Rikyu's descendants still teach it.

Glassblowing in the Roman World People in Mesopotamia and Egypt were making glass objects more than three thousand years ago, but for most of that time glass was rare and expensive. Craftsmen shaped it by pouring melted glass into molds or by winding hot threads of glass around a core of clay. These slow methods produced small, colorful beads and bottles that only the wealthy could afford. Around the first century BCE, craftsmen on the eastern coast of the Mediterranean discovered that they could blow air through a hollow metal tube into a blob of melted glass, inflating it like a bubble. This technique, glassblowing, allowed a skilled worker to make a cup or bottle in minutes rather than hours. The new method spread quickly across the Roman Empire, and workshops appeared in Italy, Gaul, and along the Rhine. As production became faster and cheaper, glass entered ordinary Roman homes. Families used glass jars to store food and wine, and because glass could be clear, people could see what was inside without opening the container. Wealthy Romans even began to fit small panes of glass into windows. Archaeologists find fragments of Roman glass at sites across Europe, evidence of how widely the new technology was adopted.

prompt.en: 12. Write for an Academic Discussion (10 minutes) Your professor is teaching a class on education. Write a post responding to the professor's question. In your response, you should do the following: • Express and support your opinion. • Make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words. Dr. Ramsay: Some professors have banned laptops and tablets in their lectures, saying that students who take notes by hand pay more attention and remember more, and that screens distract nearby classmates. Others say that students should be trusted to choose how they learn, and that some students need devices to keep up. Should professors be allowed to ban laptops in lectures? Why or why not? Anika: I support the bans. In my big lecture classes, half the laptops in front of me are showing social media or games, and it's hard not to look. A ban would help everyone focus. Bastian: I disagree. I type much faster than I write, so I can record more of what the professor says. Students are adults, and if they waste their time online, that's their own responsibility. ______________________________________________________________________________________ ______________________________________________________________________________________ ______________________________________________________________________________________ ______________________________________________________________________________________ ______________________________________________________________________________________ ______________________________________________________________________________________ ______________________________________________________________________________________ ______________________________________________________________________________________ ______________________________________________________________________________________ ______________________________________________________________________________________ ______________________________________________________________________________________ ______________________________________________________________________________________ Section 4: Speaking 11 items · about 8 minutes Speaking Listen and Repeat: 7 items · Take an Interview: 4 items
